public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 372

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/372](https://www.erdosproblems.com/372)

Conjectured by Erdős and Pomerance. Proved by Balog, who showed the stronger quantitative result
that this holds for $\gg \sqrt{x}$ many $n\leq x$, for all large $x$.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos372

/--
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. There are infinitely many $n$ such that
$P(n)>P(n+1)>P(n+2)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_372 :
    {n : ℕ | Nat.maxPrimeFac n > Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) ∧
      Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) > Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 2)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos372

reformulations.difference: The Lean set ranges over every n : ℕ, including 0 and 1. It uses `Nat.maxPrimeFac`, which returns placeholder ('junk') values `maxPrimeFac 0 = 0` and `maxPrimeFac 1 = 1`. The source's P(n) is the largest prime factor of a positive integer; Erdős–Pomerance define it for n ≥ 2. Balog's abstract writes the pattern with shifted indices: P(n−1) > P(n) > P(n+1).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: n = 0 and n = 1 are not in the Lean set, because 0 > 1 and 1 > 2 are false (checked with `decide +kernel`). For n ≥ 1 we have n+1 ≥ 2 and n+2 ≥ 3, and for n ≥ 2 all three arguments are ≥ 2. So `Nat.maxPrimeFac_eq_sSup` makes `maxPrimeFac` equal the true largest prime factor at every argument that matters. In a scratch file I proved `sets_eq`: the file's set equals {n | 0 < n ∧ P n > P (n+1) ∧ P (n+1) > P (n+2)} with P m := sSup {p | p.Prime ∧ p ∣ m}. I also proved that this P m is the largest prime factor for m ≥ 2. `#print axioms` shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, so the proof uses no `sorry`. The two infinitude statements are therefore equivalent. In any case, infinitude is unaffected by finitely many boundary values or by an index shift.

review.notes:
The file has one declaration. `erdos_372` states `{n : ℕ | P n > P (n+1) ∧ P (n+1) > P (n+2)}.Infinite` with P = `Nat.maxPrimeFac`. That is word for word the claim on erdosproblems.com/372: "Let P(n) denote the largest prime factor of n. There are infinitely many n such that P(n)>P(n+1)>P(n+2)". The site's revision history shows no substantive change to this wording. The claim is also the open problem (20) in §7 of Erdős–Pomerance 1978: "we cannot find infinitely many n for which P(n)>P(n+1)>P(n+2)". Balog (2001) proved it; his abstract says the pattern "occurs for infinitely many integers n".

Checks I ran:
- `#eval` of `Nat.maxPrimeFac` on 0–19 gives the expected values.
- The Lean membership predicate reproduces the OEIS A071870 data section exactly, and all 1000 terms of the b-file up to 6382 (starting 13, 14, 34, ...). So the direction of the inequalities is correct.
- The placeholder values at 0 and 1 add no members; this is proved in Lean and recorded under reformulations.

Metadata: `@[category research solved]` matches the source's PROVED status (Balog 2001; see also Kim 2020 and Tao–Teräväinen). There is no `formal_proof` claim, which is optional. `AMS 11` is appropriate. Both docstrings agree with the source.

The source's remarks mention three results the file leaves out: Balog's ≫√x lower bound, Balog's conjectured density of 1/6, and De Koninck–Doyon's generalisation. That is an omission, not a defect in the existing declaration.

`git status` shows a modified `lakefile.toml` and an untracked `run/` directory. Neither was touched by me; the file under review is unmodified.
